consensus_summary: All four blind responses converge on the Sabbath as symbolizing rest: God's creation rest typologically fulfilled as spiritual rest/salvation in Christ and ultimately eschatological rest (Hebrews 3-4, Colossians 2:16-17, Matthew 11:28-30). Alternatives include covenant-sign of Israel, continuing seventh-day observance, transfer to the Lord's Day, millennial-week typology, and liberation/social-justice readings. In every case the referent is the seventh-day rest itself and what that rest signifies.
book_summary: The book identifies the Sabbath not as the rest day itself but as 'a complete seven crowned by rest' — the whole seven-unit at every scale the law counts: the week, the land's seventh year, the seven sevens to Jubilee. It marshals linguistic evidence that Hebrew counts spans in 'sabbaths' (Lev 23:15; 25:8) where Deuteronomy counts 'weeks,' and that Greek sabbaton denotes the week itself (dis tou sabbatou = twice a week, mia sabbatōn = first day of the week). The rest is only 'the completing member of the whole unit.' Its common-view note explicitly rejects the standard identification: 'the day, not the seven it completes.'
consensus_core_identification: Sabbath = the seventh-day rest, symbolizing participation in God's rest, fulfilled as rest in Christ and eschatological rest.
book_core_identification: Sabbath = the complete unit of seven itself (week, seventh year, Jubilee cycle), of which the rest is merely the completing final member — not the rest day alone.
boundary_disagreement: The book reclassifies the rest day from being the referent of 'sabbath' to being one member (the crown) of the true referent, the seven-unit. It adds cases the consensus never treats as 'the Sabbath' — the week as such, the sabbatical year as a unit, the 49-year Jubilee span counted in 'sabbaths of years' — while demoting the consensus's central case (the day of rest and its Christological fulfillment) to a component role.
material_contradiction: The book's common-view note directly denies the consensus identification: the Sabbath is 'the seven it completes,' not 'the seventh-day rest itself — the day.' The consensus says the Sabbath is the rest (and symbolizes rest in Christ); the book says the Sabbath is the completed seven, with rest as merely its completing member. Both cannot be the term's central identification in the same sense; accepting the book requires replacing, not just adjusting, the consensus referent.
rationale: Although rest remains present in the book's formulation ('crowned by rest'), the central identification shifts from rest-as-referent to completeness-of-seven-as-referent. No blind response or listed alternative treats the Sabbath as the whole week/seven-unit; the closest (millennial cosmic-week typology) still treats the Sabbath as the seventh member, not the unit. The book explicitly frames itself against the common teaching, and its extension (weeks, sabbatical years, Jubilee cycles counted as 'sabbaths') differs materially from the consensus's extension (the rest day and its spiritual/eschatological fulfillments). This is replacement of the central referent, not boundary refinement, so DIVERGENT rather than REFINED; it is not NOVEL because the book positions itself as contradicting an identifiable consensus, not merely filling a gap.
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's category (Sabbath bound up with rest and the seven-day pattern rooted in creation) and merely broadens the referent from the day to the unit it completes, and its Heb 4:9 citation shows it retains the eschatological-rest dimension. The Hebrew and Greek usage it cites (Lev 23:15; Lev 25:8; Luke 18:12; Matt 28:1) genuinely shows 'sabbath' denoting week-spans, so the book could be read as recovering an extended lexical sense rather than contradicting the symbolic consensus. However, the explicit 'the day, not the seven it completes' framing marks replacement of the central identification, tipping the verdict to DIVERGENT.
